reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India national programmes
clinicalPearls: A protozoal infection caused by Cryptosporidium species, transmitted faecal-orally through contaminated water, food or contact, with a very low infectious dose
In immunocompetent hosts it causes a self-limiting watery diarrhoea, but in the immunocompromised, especially advanced HIV, it can cause severe, chronic and life-threatening diarrhoea
A recognised cause of waterborne outbreaks because the oocysts are highly resistant to routine chlorination
An important contributor to childhood diarrhoea and to malnutrition and growth faltering in Indian children
In profound immunosuppression infection may extend beyond the gut to the biliary tract, causing sclerosing cholangitis, and to the respiratory tract
Restoration of immune function, particularly antiretroviral therapy in HIV, is central to control in immunocompromised patients
Diagnosis requires specific tests: modified acid-fast staining of stool, antigen detection or PCR, as the oocysts are missed on routine microscopy
Management emphasises rehydration; antiprotozoal drug options are limited and work best when immunity is restored
reference.pathophysiology: Ingested Cryptosporidium oocysts release sporozoites that invade the apical surface of intestinal epithelial cells, residing in an intracellular but extracytoplasmic compartment. Infection blunts villi, impairs absorption and increases secretion, producing a watery, non-bloody diarrhoea. In immunocompetent people a robust cellular immune response clears the parasite, but when T-cell immunity is deficient the organism proliferates unchecked, causing high-volume chronic diarrhoea, malabsorption and spread to biliary and respiratory epithelium.
additionalDifferentials: Other opportunistic enteric infections in HIV
infectionMimics: Other opportunistic causes of chronic diarrhoea in advanced HIV
Small bowel malabsorption of non-infective cause
additionalInvestigations: Modified acid-fast (Kinyoun) staining of stool for oocysts
Stool antigen detection or PCR for sensitive diagnosis
HIV testing and CD4 count assessment when severe or chronic
Evaluation of hydration and electrolyte status
Imaging or biliary studies if cholangiopathy is suspected in the immunocompromised
redFlags: Severe or high-volume dehydrating diarrhoea, especially in infants or the immunocompromised
Chronic diarrhoea with weight loss in a patient with advanced HIV/AIDS
Right upper quadrant pain and cholestasis suggesting biliary involvement
Failure of diarrhoea to settle, signalling underlying immunodeficiency
reference.prognosis: In immunocompetent individuals the illness resolves spontaneously over one to two weeks. In severely immunocompromised patients it can be chronic, debilitating and fatal unless immune function is restored, and outcome is closely tied to recovery of cellular immunity.
pitfalls: Failing to request specific staining, antigen or PCR tests, so oocysts are missed on routine stool microscopy
Not testing for HIV in a patient with severe or persistent cryptosporidial diarrhoea
Relying on antiprotozoal drugs alone in the immunocompromised without addressing the underlying immune deficit
Underestimating waterborne outbreak potential given oocyst resistance to chlorination
management: Oral or intravenous rehydration and electrolyte correction as the mainstay of supportive care
Nitazoxanide antiparasitic therapy to shorten illness, most useful in immunocompetent and malnourished hosts
Restoration of cellular immunity is central in the immunocompromised, above all antiretroviral therapy to raise the CD4 count in HIV
Nutritional support and attention to growth faltering in affected children
Manage biliary complications such as sclerosing cholangitis, including endoscopic intervention, when infection spreads beyond the gut
Infection-control and public-health measures including hand hygiene, boiling or filtering water and avoiding swimming, recognising oocysts resist chlorination
Escalate for severe dehydration, high-volume chronic diarrhoea or extra-intestinal spread

Brucellosis (Brucella spp.); epsilon toxin of Clostridium perfringens; food safety threats (for example Salmonella spp., Escherichia coli O157:H7, Shigella); glanders (Burkholderia mallei); melioidosis (B. pseudomallei); psittacosis (Chlamydophila psittaci); Q fever (Coxiella burnetii); ricin toxin from Ricinus communis (castor beans); staphylococcal enterotoxin B; typhus fever (Rickettsia prowazekii); viral encephalitis [alphaviruses, for example Venezuelan, eastern and western equine encephalitis]; water safety threats (for example Vibrio cholerae, Cryptosporidium parvum)
Emerging infectious disease threats such as Nipah, hantavirus, SARS coronavirus and pandemic influenza
